newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST-API heat draw seen with unseasonable cold.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-API heat draw seen with unseasonable cold.

text.p: The American Petroleum Institute (API) is expected by traders to report a minor draw in distillate stocks in its oil inventory data Tuesday evening as unseasonably cold weather in the U.S. has drained supply.
"We have seen some late season tightness in heating oil supply with some cold weather in the (U.S.) Midwest and East," said Richard Redash, analyst with Prudential Securities.
Traders were expecting the API data, which reflects the week ended May 2, to show distillate stocks flat to down one million barrels versus the week ago.

Distillate stocks are comprised of heating oil and diesel. Before going off the board Wednesday last week, May heating oil rose five cents a gallon five sessions before the day of expiry on supply tightness in the New York Harbor cash market.

Meteorologists said this spring's temperatures have trended below normal as a whole. Also, analysts said a shift in refinery output toward gasoline and away from distillate ahead of the summer driving season has limited heat supply.
But, traders said cash tightness is temporary with warmer temperatures already hitting the key heating oil market of the northeastern United States.

"When we do enter the fourth quarter, we will be in a much better position with distillate supplies than we were last year," said William Brown, president of W.H. Brown & Co, a trading firm in New York.
Brown noted heating oil stocks are still running at a surplus versus a year ago in the Northeast region.
Crude stocks are seen rising one to three million barrels, extending several consecutive weeks of builds driven by imports from across the Atlantic.

"The arbitrage is still providing an incentive for imports and at least until the European refineries complete their turnaround cycles, cargoes are not all that hard to come by," said Tim Evans, analyst with Pegasus Econometric Research, in a daily report.
Gasoline stocks are expected to rise one to two million barrels as implied demand has stayed above a lofty eight million barrels a day over the past two weeks of data.
"I expect us to have a slight correction to the gasoline demand we have been seeing to more realistic levels," said Jim Ritterbusch, trader with Sweeney Oil in Illinois.

Also a factor driving the anticipated increase in gasoline supply is an expected rise in refinery utilization by about 0.50 percentage point from the 93.5 percent reported in last week's data. An uptick in Midwest run rates should drive the overall utilization rise.
"The (refinery run) rate has been too low in the Midwest, at around 88 to 89 percent, so I expect that to rise a bit," said Ritterbusch.
